paragraphs: Swamiji begins with how poetry itself was born. The sage Valmiki, on his way to bathe in the Ganga, was enjoying the sight of two doves playing together when a hunter's arrow killed the male. As the female circled her dead mate in grief, Valmiki burst out in angry verse against the cruel hunter, and was startled by his own words. A divine voice told him not to fear: this was poetry, and he should use it to tell the life of Rama for the good of the world.

In Ayodhya, King Dasharatha and his three queens prayed for children and were blessed with four sons, Rama the eldest. Rama won the hand of Sita, the earth-born daughter of King Janaka, by snapping the mighty bow that every other prince had failed even to bend. But on the eve of Rama's crowning, Queen Kaikeyi, stirred up by a jealous maidservant, claimed two old promises from the king: her son Bharata on the throne, and Rama in the forest for fourteen years. To save his father from breaking his word, Rama cheerfully gave up everything. Sita insisted on coming, and so did the loyal Lakshmana.

In the forest, the demon king Ravana used a magic golden deer to lure Rama away, tricked Sita out of Lakshmana's protective circle by posing as a hungry monk, and carried her off to Lanka. She dropped her ornaments as a trail. Rama found allies in Sugriva and the devoted Hanuman, who leapt across the sea, found Sita pale and unshaken under a tree, and brought back her jewel. As the monkeys hurled hills into the sea to build a bridge, a tiny squirrel rolled in the sand and shook it onto the bridge. The others laughed, but Rama blessed it and stroked its back, and the marks of his fingers, it is said, remain on squirrels to this day.

Ravana fell, Lanka was given to his brother Vibhishana, and Rama returned to rule. Yet the people kept doubting Sita. She passed through fire unharmed, and still, bowing to public opinion, the king had to banish her. In Valmiki's hermitage she gave birth to twin sons, Lava and Kusha, whom the sage trained to sing the Ramayana.

Years later, when Rama was told to remarry for a great sacrifice, he refused, for his life belonged to Sita, and used a golden statue of her instead. At that festival the boys sang their father's story. When Sita was brought forward and the cry for another test rose again, she called on the gods and the Earth opened to receive her. Soon Rama, his mission complete, entered the Sarayu river to join her.
For Swamiji, Sita is the ideal of India: pure, devoted, enduring. The West says show your power by doing; India, he says, has also learned to show it by suffering.
learn: Rama's quiet sacrifice and Sita's steady strength show that character is proven in hard moments, not easy ones. And the squirrel reminds us that a small effort, given fully, counts as much as a great one.
